messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq was fifty-two when he finally walked into a clinic, but the weight of his symptoms had been building for nearly a decade. It began at the old Meridian Theatre, during a dress rehearsal where a collapsed lighting grid killed his younger brother, Layth. Tariq had been in the front row, watching as steel cables snapped without warning. The event never played out as a continuous narrative for him; instead, he experienced photographic recalls of Layth pinned beneath the wreckage, followed instantly by fragmented pieces of scattered rigging and his brother’s stunned face. When those disconnected images surfaced with their accompanying guilt, Tariq felt compelled to surrender his own boundaries, going along with whatever his directors or casting agents demanded just to feel momentarily safe, while his isolation in empty rooms only allowed the memories to replay louder. Digging through the aftermath, he learned the theater company had buried hazard reports and quietly signed off on the equipment. The official inquiry cleared everyone. No accountability was ever pursued, and Tariq had come to believe the institutions that should have protected them had fundamentally let him down. Over the following months, ordinary stimuli became relentless entry points into that trauma. A radio news segment about a venue fire would instantly pull him back to the Meridian, conjuring the same flash-like memories of the collapse. Even subtle auditory cues—a dropped set piece, a sudden clatter backstage, or the distant wail of a child in a grocery aisle—sped up his pulse and triggered those photographic flashes. These sensory shocks did not stop at fear; they cemented his conviction that the institutions guarding public spaces were fundamentally compromised, locking his inaction guilt in place. Because his negative emotions and inability to trust safety ran so high, he became hyper-vigilant to media and ambient sounds, which in turn sparked the next wave of panic. When the sensory shocks spiked his heart rate, Tariq felt forced to flee crowded venues like shopping centers or public theaters, telling himself these habits were just career boundaries when they were really flight responses to a threat system that could not be switched off. The avoidance and appeasement only sharpened his internal alarm. Every time the memories surfaced, the guilt on recall tightened his chest, and the negative emotions that followed—horror, shame, and paralyzing fear—made it impossible for him to concentrate on script lines. Because he could not trust that safety was real, even when agents swore the new inspections were thorough, Tariq felt compelled to avoid being alone in any room or building after dark. The negative appraisals of institutional failure and inaction guilt compounded the threat; if the system had abandoned Layth once, it would abandon him too, and he would be forever responsible for not preventing it. The paralysis of fear and shame reinforced his belief that the system had failed them and would never change, while continuing to appease everyone and avoid crowds only convinced him that he lacked the agency to demand justice, reinforcing his negative appraisal that no accountability would ever come. At fifty-two, the loop had become the architecture of his days. A director’s casual mention of “the old warehouse stage” would trigger a cascade: the memory of Layth’s pinned shoulder would flash, the inability to trust safety would spike his heart rate, and the conviction that the system had abandoned them once would lock his throat shut. His constant people-pleasing had cost him his marriage; his late wife had left years ago, unable to tolerate a husband who flinched at children crying in the grocery aisle or who refused to share a quiet dinner alone. The fewer crowds he navigated, the less tolerance he had for unexpected noise, meaning everyday background sounds suddenly felt as dangerous as the collapse itself. This constant hypervigilance kept his concentration shattered and his guilt and shame at a boil, making safety feel perpetually out of reach while the cycle fed on itself. What finally brought him to a clinic was a near-collapse during a monologue rehearsal, where the lights dimmed and he was certain the grid was groaning again. He sought help not to forget Layth, but to break the suffocating cycle where every sound, every crowd, and every quiet moment only proved to him that the world was unsafe, the system was corrupt, and his guilt was a permanent sentence.
